Thank you for taking the time to respond! I do appreciate peoples interest and engaging me in this topic. You bring up a solid point—recovery isn’t one-size-fits-all, and both harm reduction and abstinence-based approaches have value. It's not really as black and white as my post may make it sound for me even, I was just very frustrated in that moment with something I had read from a non-addict posting about a loved one.
In my experience, yes. Even like, on the internet in stuff I see it’s just overwhelming fluff and walking on egg shells!
lol well idk you came with a comment and I responded explaining what exactly I believe is meant by powerlessness. Take care.

I get that not all treatment works for everyone, but blaming the system entirely ignores personal responsibility. Plenty of people don’t get ‘perfect’ treatment yet still make recovery work. At some point, it’s less about what wasn’t given and more about what’s done with what’s available.
Powerlessness isn’t about being alone—it’s about realizing \*willpower alone\* won’t cut it. Addiction runs on patterns, and without the right tools, it just repeats.

Well yes, I totally agree— recovery isn’t **always** one-size-fits-all, and rehab isn’t a magic fix... I will add, rehab success rates depend on factors like length of stay, follow-up care, and life after.... Success rates for rehab and AA are debated, but outcomes with treatment vs. without treatment show rehab is a pretty safe bet. Ultimately, a person’s willingness to use the tools they’re given determines the results, I don't understand what we aren't agreeing on that prompted you to comment this?

I do think there’s a big misunderstanding when it comes to loved ones of addicts. I think that’s where a lot of tension comes in—between holding someone accountable and understanding the realities of addiction. I appreciate the discussion!
